notes: One entry per ALLERGEN_VOCABULARY token (src/lib/allergens.ts). Regulatory facts are stated only where well established: the US list is FALCPA's eight plus sesame under the FASTER Act (labelling from 1 January 2023); the EU list is the fourteen in Annex II of Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011. Anything less certain is marked unverified in the text. No brands, no restaurant names, no medical thresholds, no severity claims, no absence-guarantee wording. Validated by scripts/seed-allergens-ai.ts --from-file against AllergenReferenceSchema; every row lands published=false for editorial review.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004 and on the EU Annex II list, where it is listed as milk including lactose. Both lists apply to milk from any mammal, not only cows.

hiddenSources.product: Deli meats, hot dogs and sausages
hiddenSources.why: Casein or milk powder is used as a binder and filler in some processed meats.
Many are built on sodium caseinate, a milk protein, even though the product is labelled non-dairy.
Some brands pack tuna in a broth that contains hydrolysed casein.
Milk powder, butter or whey is common in enriched doughs and glazes.

hiddenSources.product: Instant mashed potatoes and boxed potato mixes
hiddenSources.why: Milk solids and butter powder are standard in the mix.
Milk solids are an ingredient in most milk chocolate and many dark chocolates, and caramel is usually made with butter or cream.
Whey and casein are the most common protein sources in these products.
Batters and breadings often contain milk or buttermilk, and some are fried in butter.
Buttermilk, sour cream, yogurt or cheese form the base.
Lactose is a common filler in tablets and capsules; check with a pharmacist.
The lactose is broken down but the milk proteins remain.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction to goat's and sheep's milk is commonly reported alongside cow's milk allergy, because the proteins are closely related. A relationship with beef is reported less often. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask what the pan was greased with and whether the dish is finished with butter or cream; both are routine in restaurant kitchens and rarely appear on a menu. Ask whether mashed potatoes, bread, breading, risotto and soups contain milk, butter, cream or cheese. Menu words that usually mean milk: au gratin, alfredo, bechamel, buttermilk, brulee, carbonara, ghee, paneer, queso, ranch, tzatziki. Non-dairy and lactose-reduced on a label do not mean the milk proteins are absent. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004 and on the EU Annex II list. Both cover eggs from any bird, not only hens.

hiddenSources.why: Egg yolk is the emulsifier in traditional versions.
The dough is made with whole eggs or yolks.

hiddenSources.product: Egg wash on breads, pastries, pretzels and pies
hiddenSources.why: Beaten egg is brushed on before baking for shine and colour.

hiddenSources.product: Meatballs, meatloaf, burgers and crab cakes
hiddenSources.why: Egg is a common binder in mixed and formed meats.
Whipped egg white gives these their structure.
Sours and fizzes are often shaken with egg white.
Egg yolk is the base of these sauces.
Lysozyme, an egg-white protein, is used as a preservative in some Italian-style hard cheeses.
Egg white is a traditional fining agent used to clarify wine.
Egg yolks thicken the base.

hiddenSources.product: Fried rice and some noodle dishes
hiddenSources.why: Scrambled egg is stirred through and easy to miss.
Egg is the usual glue between the food and the breading.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction to the eggs of other birds, such as duck and quail, is commonly reported alongside hen's egg allergy. An association with bird feathers and poultry meat is reported but less common. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether breads and pastries were brushed with egg wash, whether burgers, meatballs or crab cakes use egg as a binder, and whether the pasta is fresh egg pasta or dried. Ask about the dressing on salads and the sauce on eggs benedict, fish and steak, since hollandaise, bearnaise, Caesar and aioli are all egg based. Menu words that usually mean egg: meringue, custard, souffle, frittata, carbonara, tempura, brioche, challah, aioli. At a bar, ask whether a cocktail is shaken with egg white. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

alternateNames: fish sauce (nam pla, nuoc mam, patis)

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004, which requires the species to be named (for example cod, salmon, tuna); on the EU Annex II list as fish. Annex II exempts fish gelatine used as a carrier for vitamins and fish gelatine or isinglass used to clarify beer and wine from the declaration.

hiddenSources.why: Anchovy is a traditional ingredient, and the sauce turns up in marinades, burgers, Caesar dressing and cocktails.
Anchovy is part of the classic recipe.

hiddenSources.product: Thai, Vietnamese and Filipino dishes and dipping sauces
hiddenSources.why: Fish sauce is a foundational seasoning, including in many dishes that contain no visible fish.
Dashi is usually made from bonito, a dried fish, and underlies miso soup, ramen, noodle broths and many sauces.
Made from minced white fish, usually pollock.

hiddenSources.product: Puttanesca, tapenade and some pizza toppings
hiddenSources.why: Anchovy is blended into the sauce or paste.
Many recipes use fish sauce or fermented anchovy.
Isinglass, made from fish swim bladders, is used to clarify them.

hiddenSources.product: Gummy candies, marshmallows and softgel supplements
hiddenSources.why: Some use fish gelatin instead of pork or beef gelatin.
Anchovy or Worcestershire sauce adds savoury depth.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction across several species of fish is commonly reported, because many fish share a similar muscle protein. Fish and shellfish are separate allergen categories on both the US and EU lists, and a reaction to one is not treated as a reaction to the other. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether a dish contains fish sauce, anchovy, dashi or Worcestershire sauce, since all four are used as seasonings in dishes that show no fish. Ask whether fried foods share oil with fish, and whether the grill or plancha is shared. In Thai, Vietnamese, Japanese and Korean restaurants, ask specifically about fish sauce and dashi in vegetable dishes and soups. Menu words to check: Caesar, puttanesca, nicoise, dashi, bonito, surimi, nam pla, Worcestershire. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004, listed there as crustacean shellfish with the species named (for example crab, lobster, shrimp); on the EU Annex II list as crustaceans. Molluscs such as oysters, clams and squid are a separate EU entry and are not on the US list at all.

hiddenSources.why: Shrimp paste is a standard ingredient in red, green and many other curry pastes.

hiddenSources.product: Sambals and Southeast Asian chili sauces
hiddenSources.why: Fermented shrimp paste (belacan or terasi) is often the base.
Salted fermented shrimp is a common seasoning.
Made from dried shrimp and dried scallop.

hiddenSources.product: Instant noodle and ramen seasoning packets
hiddenSources.why: Seafood-flavoured versions often contain shrimp powder.

hiddenSources.product: Pork or vegetable dumplings, wontons and spring rolls
hiddenSources.why: Minced shrimp is often mixed into the filling.
Dried shrimp is stirred through for flavour and is easy to miss.
Shells are simmered for the base, even in dishes served without visible shellfish.
Shrimp or crawfish is usually part of the base.
Often made from the shells of shrimp and crab.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction across several crustaceans (shrimp, crab, lobster) is commonly reported, and a relationship between crustaceans and molluscs is also commonly reported, because both groups share a muscle protein called tropomyosin. An association with dust mites and cockroaches, which carry a related protein, is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether curry pastes, sambals, fried rice, dumplings and stocks contain shrimp or shrimp paste, since these are seasonings rather than visible pieces. Ask whether the wok, grill, fryer or steamer is shared with shellfish, and whether a seafood boil or platter is prepared on the same surfaces. Menu words to check: scampi, langoustine, bisque, etouffee, tom yum, nam prik, belacan, XO, surf and turf. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004, which requires the specific nut to be named; on the EU Annex II list as nuts, which names eight: almond, hazelnut, walnut, cashew, pecan, Brazil nut, pistachio and macadamia. The two lists do not match: pine nuts, chestnuts and coconut are not on the EU nuts entry, and the FDA revised its own tree-nut list in recent guidance, so which of those the US list currently includes should be treated as unverified here and checked against the FDA's current guidance.

hiddenSources.why: Traditionally made with pine nuts, and often with cashews or walnuts in place of them.

hiddenSources.product: Romesco, mole and some Mexican and Spanish sauces
hiddenSources.why: Ground almonds, hazelnuts or other nuts thicken and flavour the sauce.

hiddenSources.product: Korma and other creamy Indian curries
hiddenSources.why: Cashew or almond paste is the base of the sauce.

hiddenSources.product: Marzipan, frangipane, macarons and almond pastries
hiddenSources.why: Made from ground almonds or almond flour.
Layered with walnuts, pistachios or almonds.
Hazelnuts or almonds are the defining ingredient.
Orgeat is an almond syrup used in tiki and sour drinks.

hiddenSources.product: Plant-based cheeses, milks, yogurts and ice creams
hiddenSources.why: Many are built on cashews or almonds.
Nuts and nut butters are common ingredients and shared lines are common.
Ground nuts replace breadcrumbs in the coating.

hiddenSources.product: Some salad dressings and grain salads
hiddenSources.why: Walnut or hazelnut oil, or a nut garnish, is added.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction across several tree nuts is commonly reported, with cashew and pistachio, and walnut and pecan, the pairs reported most often. A relationship between tree nuts and peanuts is commonly reported even though peanuts are legumes. An association between birch pollen and hazelnut or almond is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether sauces contain nut pastes, ground nuts or nut oils, since pesto, romesco, mole, korma and many dressings hide them. Ask about garnishes on salads, desserts and vegetable dishes, and about shared equipment in bakeries, ice cream shops (scoops) and dessert stations. Menu words to check: pesto, romesco, korma, satay, praline, marzipan, frangipane, macaron, gianduja, crusted, amaretti, orgeat. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004 and on the EU Annex II list. US law exempts highly refined oils, including highly refined peanut oil, from allergen labelling; the EU list has no equivalent exemption for peanut oil. Peanuts are legumes, listed separately from tree nuts on both lists.

hiddenSources.product: Satay, peanut sauces and many Thai, Vietnamese and Indonesian dishes
hiddenSources.why: Ground peanuts or peanut butter form the sauce, and crushed peanuts are a standard garnish.

hiddenSources.product: Mole and some chili and stew recipes
hiddenSources.why: Ground peanuts thicken and flavour the sauce.
Peanut butter is sometimes used to seal the wrapper.
Peanut paste is the base of the dish.
Peanuts are cooked into the dish, not only sprinkled on top.

hiddenSources.product: Granola, cereal bars and trail mix
hiddenSources.why: Peanuts or peanut butter are common ingredients and shared lines are common.

hiddenSources.product: Baked goods, candy and ice cream
hiddenSources.why: Peanut butter fillings, swirls and shared equipment are common.
Peanut protein or flour adds protein.

hiddenSources.product: Sunflower seed butter and other seed butters
hiddenSources.why: Often made on equipment shared with peanut butter.
Peanut oil or peanut butter adds body and flavour.

entries.crossReactivity: A relationship between peanuts and tree nuts is commonly reported even though peanuts are legumes. Reaction to other legumes, most often lupin, and less often soy, fenugreek, lentils or chickpeas, is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask what oil the fryer uses, since some restaurants fry in peanut oil, and whether sauces, dressings and garnishes contain peanuts or peanut butter. Ask whether woks and grills are shared with peanut dishes. In Thai, Vietnamese, Chinese, Indonesian, Mexican and West African restaurants, ask specifically about peanuts in sauces and stews that show no whole peanuts. Menu words to check: satay, kung pao, pad thai, mole, groundnut, gado-gado, bun cha. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

alternateNames: flour (all-purpose, bread, cake, pastry, whole wheat, graham, enriched)

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004; on the EU Annex II list as part of the entry for cereals containing gluten, which names wheat together with spelt and khorasan wheat. Annex II exempts wheat-based glucose syrups, dextrose and maltodextrins from the declaration. US law covers wheat alone; barley and rye are not US-listed allergens, so a US wheat-allergen label says nothing about other gluten-containing grains.

hiddenSources.why: Most soy sauce is brewed with roasted wheat, so it appears in marinades, dressings and many Asian dishes.
Seitan is wheat gluten; other substitutes use wheat protein as a binder.
Wheat starch is a common binder.
A flour roux or wheat-based thickener is standard.

hiddenSources.product: Sausages, meatballs, burgers and processed meats
hiddenSources.why: Breadcrumbs or wheat flour are used as filler and binder.
These are wheat products even though they are not called wheat.
Wheat flour is a main ingredient in traditional licorice.
Wheat beers use wheat; most beers use barley, which is not the same allergen but is a gluten cereal.

hiddenSources.product: Some ice creams and frozen desserts
hiddenSources.why: Cookie dough, brownie, cake and malt mix-ins contain wheat.

hiddenSources.product: Spice blends, seasonings and gravy mixes
hiddenSources.why: Wheat flour or starch is used as a carrier or anti-caking agent.
Wheat-based thickeners or malt vinegar (barley) appear in some recipes.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction to other gluten-containing grains such as barley and rye is commonly reported alongside wheat allergy. An association with grass pollen is reported. Wheat allergy is distinct from coeliac disease and from non-coeliac gluten sensitivity; which of these applies to a particular person is a medical question outside the scope of this page.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask what thickens sauces, soups and gravies, whether meat is dredged in flour before searing, and whether marinades contain soy sauce. Ask whether the fryer is shared with breaded or battered items and whether the grill is dusted with flour. Menu words to check: tempura, dredged, en croute, roux, couscous, bulgur, seitan, farro, beer-battered, teriyaki, panko. A gluten-related label on a menu is a separate claim from a wheat-allergen statement, so ask about wheat specifically. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: One of the eight allergens named in the US FALCPA law of 2004 and on the EU Annex II list. Both exempt highly refined soybean oil from allergen labelling; Annex II also exempts natural mixed tocopherols and plant sterol and stanol esters derived from soy. Soy lecithin is not exempt under US law and must be declared.

hiddenSources.product: Vegetable broth, bouillon and stock cubes
hiddenSources.why: Soy protein or hydrolysed soy protein is a common savoury base.
Often packed in vegetable broth that contains soy.

hiddenSources.product: Processed meats, veggie burgers and meat substitutes
hiddenSources.why: Soy protein is the most common plant protein used as filler or main ingredient.
Soy flour improves texture and soy lecithin is a near-universal emulsifier in chocolate.

hiddenSources.product: Asian sauces: soy sauce, tamari, hoisin, teriyaki, miso, ponzu
hiddenSources.why: All are made from soybeans, and tamari is soy even though it is sold as a wheat-free soy sauce.
Generic vegetable oil in North America is often soybean oil, though highly refined oil is exempt from labelling.
Soy protein isolate is a common protein source.
Soybean oil is the usual base oil.

hiddenSources.product: Worcestershire sauce and some barbecue sauces
hiddenSources.why: Some recipes include soy sauce or soy protein.

hiddenSources.product: Some peanut butters and nut butters
hiddenSources.why: Soybean oil is added as a stabiliser in some brands.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction to other legumes, including peanuts and lupin, is reported alongside soy allergy. An association between birch pollen and soy is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether marinades, dressings and sauces contain soy sauce, miso or tamari, and what oil the kitchen fries in, since generic vegetable oil is often soybean oil. Ask whether tofu, edamame or tempeh is used in dishes where it is not obvious, such as dressings and desserts. Menu words to check: shoyu, tamari, teriyaki, miso, ponzu, hoisin, tempeh, yuba, plant-based protein. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: Added to the US list by the FASTER Act of 2021, with labelling required on foods from 1 January 2023, making nine US major allergens; on the EU Annex II list as sesame seeds. After the US rule took effect it was widely reported that some manufacturers began adding sesame to products such as bread so they could declare it rather than prevent cross-contact, so a US label listing sesame may reflect either.

hiddenSources.why: Tahini, a sesame paste, is a core ingredient.
Made almost entirely from sesame paste and sugar.

hiddenSources.product: Za'atar, dukkah and everything-style seasoning blends
hiddenSources.why: Sesame seeds are a standard component.

hiddenSources.product: Burger buns, bagels, breadsticks and crackers
hiddenSources.why: Seeds on top, sesame in the dough, or shared bakery lines.

hiddenSources.product: Asian dressings, marinades and stir-fry sauces
hiddenSources.why: Toasted sesame oil is a common finishing ingredient.
Sesame seeds or furikake are sprinkled over the top.
Tahini is the base.
Sesame seeds or tahini add binding and flavour.

hiddenSources.product: Rice crackers and some snack mixes
hiddenSources.why: Sesame is a common coating or ingredient.
Sesame seeds replace breadcrumbs in the crust.

entries.crossReactivity: Co-occurring reactions to sesame and to tree nuts or peanuts are commonly reported. Reaction to other seeds is reported less often. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether the bun or bread is seeded or baked on shared trays, whether salads and bowls are finished with sesame seeds or sesame oil, and whether dressings contain tahini. Ask about shared bakery equipment and toppings stations. Menu words to check: tahini, za'atar, dukkah, goma, gomae, furikake, halva, hummus, everything seasoning, sesame-crusted. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as cereals containing gluten, namely wheat (such as spelt and khorasan wheat), rye, barley, oats and their hybridised strains; Annex II exempts wheat-based glucose syrups and maltodextrins, barley-based glucose syrups and cereals used to make alcoholic distillates. There is no equivalent category in US allergen law: wheat is a US-listed allergen on its own, while barley, rye and oats are not, and US rules for a gluten-related claim on a label are a separate regulation from the allergen list.

hiddenSources.product: Beer, ale, lager and malt beverages
hiddenSources.why: Made from malted barley; wheat beers add wheat.

hiddenSources.product: Malt vinegar, malt extract and malt flavouring
hiddenSources.why: Derived from barley, and used in cereals, candies, crackers and some drinks.
Usually brewed with wheat.
Often a by-product of barley brewing and may carry barley.
Flour, barley or malt-based flavourings are common thickeners and seasonings.
Rusk, breadcrumbs or flour are used as filler.
Oats are on the EU gluten cereal list, and oats grown or milled alongside wheat commonly carry it.
Seitan is wheat gluten.

hiddenSources.product: Spice blends, seasoning packets and gravy mixes
hiddenSources.why: Wheat flour or starch is a common carrier.

hiddenSources.product: Imitation crab, some deli meats and some cheese products
hiddenSources.why: Wheat starch is used as a binder.

hiddenSources.product: Some ice cream, chocolate and candy
hiddenSources.why: Malt, cookie, wafer and cake mix-ins contain gluten cereals.

entries.crossReactivity: Wheat, barley and rye are closely related grains and reactions across them are commonly reported. Oats are listed with them in the EU because they are frequently grown and milled with wheat. A food allergy to a gluten cereal is distinct from coeliac disease and from non-coeliac gluten sensitivity; which applies to a particular person is a medical question outside the scope of this page.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask what thickens sauces, soups and gravies, whether meat is dredged in flour, whether the fryer is shared with breaded or battered items, and whether malt vinegar, beer or soy sauce is used in the dish. Ask about croutons, barley in soups, and oats in desserts and toppings. In the EU and UK, menus and allergen matrices list cereals containing gluten as a group; in the US, only wheat is tracked as an allergen, so ask about barley, rye and oats separately. Menu words to check: beer-battered, malt, au jus, seitan, farro, bulgur, panko, tempura, dredged, croutons. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as celery and products thereof, which covers the stalk, leaf, seed and root (celeriac). Not a US-listed allergen, so US labels name it only as an ordinary ingredient. Celery powder and celery juice are widely used in the US as a natural curing agent in meats labelled uncured.

hiddenSources.product: Stocks, broths, bouillon cubes and stock pastes
hiddenSources.why: Celery is part of the standard vegetable base for most stocks.

hiddenSources.product: Soups, stews, braises, risottos and sauces
hiddenSources.why: Mirepoix and soffritto, the aromatic base of countless dishes, include celery.

hiddenSources.product: Uncured bacon, hot dogs, ham and deli meats
hiddenSources.why: Celery powder or juice supplies the nitrite that cures the meat.

hiddenSources.product: Bloody Mary mix and celery-salt rims
hiddenSources.why: Celery salt and celery juice are standard.

hiddenSources.product: Seafood seasoning blends and pickling spice
hiddenSources.why: Celery seed is a defining ingredient in many blends.
Celery is a common base for its mild flavour and high water content.
Diced celery is traditional.

hiddenSources.product: Potato salad, tuna salad, chicken salad and coleslaw
hiddenSources.why: Celery or celery seed adds crunch and flavour.

hiddenSources.product: Some spice blends and seasoned salts
hiddenSources.why: Celery seed or celery salt is included.

entries.crossReactivity: An association between celery and mugwort or birch pollen is commonly reported, sometimes described as celery-mugwort-spice syndrome, and reactions to related plants such as carrot, parsley, fennel, coriander and aniseed are reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether soups, sauces, risottos and braises are made on a house stock or a bouillon base, and whether the aromatic base includes celery. Ask about celery salt on cocktail rims and celery powder in cured meats. In the EU and UK, menus and allergen matrices track celery; in the US it is rarely tracked, so ask specifically. Menu words to check: consomme, bouillon, house stock, mirepoix, remoulade, waldorf, uncured, Bloody Mary. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as mustard and products thereof. Not a US-listed allergen, so US labels name it only as an ordinary ingredient, and it can sit inside a general term such as spices in some jurisdictions; in the EU it must be named.

hiddenSources.product: Mayonnaise, aioli, vinaigrettes and salad dressings
hiddenSources.why: Mustard is a standard emulsifier and flavouring in dressings and sauces.

hiddenSources.product: Barbecue sauces, ketchup-style sauces and glazes
hiddenSources.why: Mustard powder or prepared mustard is a common component.
Mustard flour is used as a binder and seasoning.

hiddenSources.product: Curry powders and many spice blends
hiddenSources.why: Mustard seed is frequently included.
Mustard seed or powder is part of the pickling brine or sauce.

hiddenSources.product: Marinades and dry rubs for meat
hiddenSources.why: Mustard helps the rub stick and adds flavour.

hiddenSources.product: Cheese sauces and some macaroni and cheese recipes
hiddenSources.why: Mustard powder sharpens the flavour.

hiddenSources.product: Deviled eggs, potato salad and egg salad
hiddenSources.why: Prepared mustard is a standard ingredient.

hiddenSources.product: Indian dals, pickles and Bengali dishes
hiddenSources.why: Mustard seeds are tempered in oil, and mustard oil is a cooking fat.
Mustard seed is used as a topping or in the dough.

entries.crossReactivity: Reactions to related plants in the cabbage family, such as rapeseed (canola), cabbage, broccoli and turnip, are reported alongside mustard allergy, and an association with mugwort pollen is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether dressings, mayonnaise and emulsified sauces contain mustard, since it is the usual emulsifier, and whether rubs, marinades, glazes and sausages contain mustard powder. In the EU and UK, menus and allergen matrices track mustard; in the US it is rarely tracked, so ask specifically. Menu words to check: Dijon, wholegrain, honey-mustard, devilled, remoulade, piccalilli, vinaigrette, rub, glaze. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as lupin and products thereof. Not a US-listed allergen, so US labels name it only as an ordinary ingredient. Lupin flour is used in some European bakery, pasta and gluten-free products, which is where it most often appears without the word lupin on the menu.

hiddenSources.product: Gluten-free breads, pasta, pizza bases and baked goods
hiddenSources.why: Lupin flour adds protein and structure to wheat-free doughs.

hiddenSources.product: High-protein and protein-enriched breads, crackers and pasta
hiddenSources.why: Lupin protein or flour is added for protein content.

hiddenSources.product: Croissants, pastries and waffles from European bakeries
hiddenSources.why: Some recipes blend lupin flour into the dough.

hiddenSources.product: Vegan and plant-based meat, dairy and egg substitutes
hiddenSources.why: Lupin protein is used as a base in some products.
Lupin protein is one of the newer plant proteins in these products.

hiddenSources.product: Lupini beans as a snack or antipasto
hiddenSources.why: Sold pickled or brined in Mediterranean and Latin American shops, sometimes under a local name.

hiddenSources.product: Some pancake, crepe and batter mixes
hiddenSources.why: Lupin flour is blended in for colour and protein.

entries.crossReactivity: A relationship between lupin and peanut is commonly reported, and is the main reason lupin was added to the EU list; reactions to other legumes such as soy, chickpea and lentil are reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether gluten-free, high-protein or vegan bakery items, pasta and substitutes contain lupin flour or lupin protein, since those are the products most likely to use it. In the EU and UK, menus and allergen matrices track lupin; in the US it is rarely tracked, so ask specifically. Menu words to check: lupini, lupino, altramuces, tremoços, lupin flour, protein-enriched. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as molluscs and products thereof. Not a US-listed allergen: US law covers crustacean shellfish only, so molluscs appear on US labels by their ordinary ingredient name and the word shellfish on a US menu or label may mean either group.

hiddenSources.why: Made from oyster extract and used across Cantonese and many other stir-fries and marinades.
Made from dried scallop and dried shrimp.
Clam juice is an ingredient in some tomato-juice drinks and in chowders.

hiddenSources.product: Seafood stocks, fumets and paella or risotto bases
hiddenSources.why: Mussel and clam liquor is often part of the stock.

hiddenSources.product: Squid ink pasta, rice and bread
hiddenSources.why: The black colour comes from cuttlefish or squid ink.

hiddenSources.product: Mixed seafood dishes: cioppino, frutti di mare, fisherman's stews
hiddenSources.why: Clams, mussels and squid are usually included.

hiddenSources.product: Some seafood seasoning powders and instant noodle packets
hiddenSources.why: Oyster or scallop extract adds savoury depth.

hiddenSources.product: Escargot dishes and garlic butters served with them
hiddenSources.why: Snails are molluscs.
Some recipes include oysters or squid alongside salted shrimp.

entries.crossReactivity: Reaction across several molluscs is commonly reported, and a relationship between molluscs and crustaceans is commonly reported, because both share a muscle protein called tropomyosin. An association with dust mites is reported. Whether any of this applies to a particular person is a question for an allergist.
entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether stir-fries, marinades and noodle dishes contain oyster sauce or XO sauce, whether soups and rice dishes are made on a seafood stock, and whether the fryer is shared with calamari. When a menu or server says shellfish, ask whether that means crustaceans, molluscs or both. Menu words to check: vongole, frutti di mare, calamari, escargot, XO, conpoy, nero di seppia, moules, cioppino, ceviche. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.

regulatoryStatus.notes: On the EU Annex II list as sulphur dioxide and sulphites at concentrations above 10 mg/kg or 10 mg/litre expressed as total sulphur dioxide; that figure is a labelling threshold set by the regulation, not a statement about what amount affects any person. Not one of the nine US major allergens, but separate US rules require a contains-sulfites declaration on foods and wine above a similar labelling level, and US rules have prohibited sulphite treatment of fresh fruits and vegetables served raw since the 1980s. Most references treat sulphite reactions as a sensitivity rather than a classic protein allergy; that distinction is a medical question outside the scope of this page.

hiddenSources.product: Wine, cider, some beers and wine-based cocktails
hiddenSources.why: Sulphites are added as a preservative, and sauces deglazed or reduced with wine carry them too.

hiddenSources.product: Dried fruit, especially apricots, golden raisins and dried apple
hiddenSources.why: Sulphur dioxide keeps the colour bright.
Sulphites prevent browning in processed potato products.

hiddenSources.product: Shrimp and other frozen or fishmonger seafood
hiddenSources.why: Sulphites are applied to prevent black spots on shrimp shells.
Wine vinegar, pickled onions, horseradish and some relishes are preserved with sulphites.

hiddenSources.product: Bottled lemon and lime juice, grape juice and some soft drinks
hiddenSources.why: Sulphites extend shelf life.

hiddenSources.product: Maraschino cherries, glace fruit and fruit toppings
hiddenSources.why: Sulphites keep the colour and texture.
Sulphites are permitted as a preservative in some fresh sausage products in some countries.

hiddenSources.product: Molasses, some syrups and some sugars
hiddenSources.why: Sulphur dioxide is used in refining.

hiddenSources.product: Some baked goods and dough mixes
hiddenSources.why: Sulphites act as dough conditioners in some products.

entries.diningOutGuidance: Ask whether sauces are made or finished with wine, cider or wine vinegar, whether dried fruit is in salads, tagines, stuffings and desserts, and whether the potatoes arrive pre-peeled or frozen. Ask whether shrimp was treated with sulphites at the supplier, which the kitchen may need to check. Menu words to check: au vin, wine reduction, beurre blanc, chutney, maraschino, dried apricot, sultana, glace. Questions about your own reaction or what amount matters are for a doctor or allergist, not a menu.
